title: Otago and Monash analysis of Australian and New Zealand crashes links pedestrian-detecting AEB to 17% fewer pedestrian or cyclist collisions
summary: In Australian and New Zealand injury crashes from 2016 to 2023, cars with pedestrian-detecting AEB had 17% fewer pedestrian or cyclist collisions than cars without AEB.
account: M. D. Keall of the University of Otago in Wellington and S. Newstead of the Monash University Accident Research Centre in Melbourne analyzed injury crashes in Australia and New Zealand from 2016 to 2023. They classed a vehicle as having pedestrian autonomous emergency braking (PAEB) when Redbook vehicle specifications listed pedestrian avoidance with braking, and they used an induced exposure method that controlled for jurisdiction, speed limit, vehicle market group, driver age and sex, weather, light and year. Vehicles with PAEB had a 17% lower rate of pedestrian or cyclist collisions (95% CI 5% to 27%) than vehicles without any AEB. Vehicles with AEB that lacked pedestrian detection showed no reduction in these collisions. Collisions with motorcycles fell 11% with PAEB (95% CI 0% to 21%). The authors estimated that the benefit was higher at night, which differs from some other studies. Traffic Injury Prevention published the study online on 11 June 2026. The design is observational, the fitment data come from specifications, and the data held too few cyclists for a separate cyclist estimate.
purpose: Pedestrian AEB is built to extend automatic braking to people on foot and on bicycles. The fewer collisions with vulnerable road users that the study measured were that purpose.
system: Pedestrian autonomous emergency braking (PAEB), identified from the Redbook specification feature for pedestrian avoidance with braking

brief: In a study published online on 11 June 2026, M. D. Keall of the University of Otago and S. Newstead of the Monash University Accident Research Centre analyzed injury crashes in Australia and New Zealand from 2016 to 2023. Vehicles with pedestrian autonomous emergency braking had a 17% lower rate of pedestrian or cyclist collisions (95% confidence interval 5% to 27%) than vehicles without any autonomous emergency braking (AEB). Vehicles with AEB that lacked pedestrian detection showed no reduction in these collisions, which suggests that the detection accounts for the benefit.[1] The authors estimated a larger benefit at night, which differs from some other studies. The rate of collisions with motorcycles was 11% lower with pedestrian AEB, but the lower end of its 95% confidence interval is zero. The design is observational, and the authors relied on vehicle specifications to tell which vehicles had the system.[2]
